title: Two choices each. Room for everyone?
hook: Four students, four rooms, and each student is happy with two. What could go wrong?

knows: matching people to rooms, each person listing rooms they accept
doesNotKnow: that a perfect matching fails exactly when some group accepts fewer rooms than it has people

misconception: If every person accepts at least one room (here, two) and there are as many rooms as people, everyone can be housed.
objective: The learner can explain that A (1, 2), B (1, 3), C (2, 3) and D (1, 3) together accept only rooms 1, 2 and 3, a constricted set of four people and three rooms, so none of the 24 assignments houses everyone; such a group is the only thing that can block a perfect matching, and letting D also accept room 4 removes it.

claims.text: With A accepting rooms 1 and 2, B 1 and 3, C 2 and 3, and D 1 and 3, none of the 24 one-to-one assignments gives every student a room they accept; the best houses three.
claims.source: Builder's node enumeration of all 4! = 24 assignments, 2026-10-14: 0 house all four, maximum housed 3. Same survey() as Demo.tsx.

claims.text: Together the four students accept only rooms 1, 2 and 3: four people, three acceptable rooms, so one must miss out.
claims.source: Union of {1,2}, {1,3}, {2,3}, {1,3} is {1,2,3}; each student needs a different room, and 4 > 3 (pigeonhole).

claims.text: A group that together accepts fewer rooms than it has members is called a constricted set, and it is the only thing that can block a full matching (Hall's matching theorem).
claims.source: Easley & Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 10 (the term 'constricted set' and the matching theorem); P. Hall, 'On Representatives of Subsets', J. London Math. Soc. 10 (1935); D. Konig (1931). Citation from the brief; attribution for the fact-checker to confirm.

claims.text: If D also accepts room 4, 2 of the 24 assignments work.
claims.source: Builder's node enumeration, 2026-10-14: with D accepting 1, 3, 4, exactly 2 of 24 house all four (D takes 4; A, B, C take 1, 3, 2 or 2, 1, 3). Adding room 4 to any one of the four students also gives 2.

recall.question: Five people, five rooms. Three of them accept only rooms 2 and 5; the other two accept any room. Can everyone get a room they accept?
options: Only if the other two take rooms 2 and 5
recall.why: The three choosy people together accept only two rooms. Three people, two acceptable rooms: a constricted set, so someone misses out whatever the others do.
